content: Idiopathic toe walking (ITW) is a diagnosis given to otherwise healthy children who continue to walk on their toes beyond the age when a normal heel-toe gait should have developed. This diagnosis is made after excluding other medical conditions that could cause toe walking. Treatment options for ITW include both conservative and surgical interventions, depending on the child's age and the presence of limitations in ankle dorsiflexion (the upward movement of the foot towards the shin). Younger children and those without significant limitations in ankle dorsiflexion are typically managed with conservative treatments, while older children with persistent toe walking and restricted ankle dorsiflexion may require surgical procedures. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions for ITW. The review aimed to assess their impact on normalizing gait, improving ankle range of motion, reducing pain, preventing recurrence, and identifying any adverse effects. The findings were intended to guide clinicians and families in making informed decisions about treatment options, considering the financial implications of these interventions. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized trials involving participants diagnosed with ITW in the absence of other medical conditions. Participants of any age who had been toe walking for more than six months, regardless of their ability to walk with a heel-toe gait or the presence of limited ankle dorsiflexion, were considered. The primary outcome was defined as an improvement in toe walking, specifically spending more than 50% of the time walking with a heel-toe gait. Secondary outcomes included changes in active and passive ankle range of motion, pain, recurrence of ITW, and adverse events. The review identified four studies with a total of 104 participants that met the inclusion criteria. However, only one study provided data suitable for analysis. This study, conducted in Sweden, was a randomized, controlled, parallel-group trial involving 47 participants. It compared the effectiveness of serial casting combined with botulinum toxin type A (BTX) versus serial casting alone in reducing ITW. The study found that a higher proportion of participants treated with BTX showed improvement in toe walking (defined as toe walking less than 50% of the time, as reported by parents). However, the evidence was of very low certainty (risk ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 0.57 to 2.55). There was little to no difference between the two groups in passive ankle dorsiflexion range of motion, regardless of whether the knee was extended or flexed, or whether the measurement was taken on the right or left side. Similarly, there was no clear difference in the recurrence of toe walking, as assessed by the severity of toe walking on gait analysis. The study did not report outcomes related to pain or active ankle range of motion. Adverse events were reported in both groups. Calf pain occurred twice in the casting-only group and three times in the BTX group. Minor skin problems were reported three times in each group, and one participant in the BTX group experienced pain immediately after the injection. The study did not specify whether the same participants experienced multiple adverse events. Importantly, these adverse events did not affect adherence to the treatment protocols. The authors concluded that the certainty of evidence from the single study comparing serial casting with and without BTX was too low to draw definitive conclusions. Three additional studies investigated interventions such as BTX, footwear, exercises, and orthoses, but the data were insufficient to evaluate their effectiveness. Further high-quality research is needed to provide more reliable evidence on the treatment of ITW.
